metadata.note: STEM/AI concept video. Sources: Klarna press release 2024-02-27 (2.3M conversations, two-thirds of customer service chats, 'the equivalent work of 700 full-time agents'; company's own figures; release does not say the assistant moves money); Klarna CEO via Bloomberg, reported by Entrepreneur and Computing, 2025 (rehiring humans, cost-driven decisions lowered quality); Nordea press release June 2026 (5 June on Nordea's page, 6 June per CX Network; Finland's first live agentic payment, coffee tasting package on Priceless.com, Nordea Mastercard, Mastercard Agent Pay, agentic tokens, PayOS; pilot); CX Network June 2026 (ING Netherlands 2 June, concert tickets, customer approved final choice); Google Cloud 'Announcing Agent Payments Protocol (AP2)' 2025-09-16 (intent mandate, cart mandate, 'non-repudiable audit trail', no liability allocation stated). Brief's '67%' rendered as Klarna's 'two-thirds'; 'executing trades' dropped (unsourced).

beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Aishwarya from the Mycroft team. This video is about AI agents in payments: what changes when an agent stops answering questions about your money and starts moving it.

beats.narration_text: In June 2026, an AI agent in Finland bought a coffee tasting package and paid for it with a real bank card. A person gave the instructions. The agent made the purchase and the payment. It was a small order, but a new kind of transaction.

beats.role_note: Klarna Feb 2024: 2.3M chats, two-thirds, equivalent work of 700 full-time agents (own numbers); 2025 rehiring humans
beats.narration_text: Method: start with the agent most people have already met. In February 2024, Klarna said its AI assistant, built on OpenAI technology, had 2.3 million conversations in its first month: two-thirds of its customer service chats, the equivalent work of 700 full-time agents. Those are Klarna's own numbers. And in 2025, its CEO said the company was hiring human agents again, because cutting costs had driven too much of the decision, and quality had suffered.

beats.role_note: read access vs write access: wrong answer vs wrong payment; Klarna release silent on moving money
beats.narration_text: Klarna's assistant handled refunds, returns and payment questions. Its announcement doesn't say whether it could move money on its own. That's the line that matters. An agent that can only read your account can give you a wrong answer. An agent with write access, one that can pay an invoice or make a purchase, can make a wrong payment. The risk changes from a bad reply to a bad transaction.

beats.role_note: June 2026 pilots: ING concert tickets (customer approves), Nordea end-to-end; Agent Pay, agentic tokens; not yet available
beats.narration_text: That line was crossed in live tests this June. On June 2, ING in the Netherlands used Mastercard Agent Pay to buy concert tickets, with the customer approving the final choice. Days later, Nordea and Mastercard completed Finland's first live agentic payment: the agent handled the purchase and the payment end to end, from the customer's instructions. Agentic tokens kept the real card details away from the agent. Both were pilots, not services customers can use yet.

beats.role_note: AP2: intent mandate + cart mandate = non-repudiable audit trail; proof is not liability; open
beats.narration_text: So who is responsible when an agent makes a wrong payment? Google's Agent Payments Protocol, AP2, tries to make that answerable. Your request is signed as an intent mandate. Your approval of the exact items and price is signed as a cart mandate. Together they form what Google calls a non-repudiable audit trail: proof of what you asked for and what you approved. But proof isn't liability. Google's announcement doesn't say who pays when something goes wrong. That question is still open.

Your turn. Pick one payment you'd let an agent make for you, and write down its limits: the most it could spend, and what it must ask you before it pays. You've just written an intent mandate by hand.
